extracted.intended_audience: writers, journalists and anyone who composes political or expository English (especially political writers and critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical prescriptive guidance for producing clear, honest, and effective English prose, with special attention to political writing and common contemporary abuses. Emphasizes concreteness, precision, and avoidance of stale, pretentious, or evasive language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dying metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid worn-out metaphors that have lost evocative power and are used merely because they save the trouble of inventing fresh phrasing; incompatible metaphors are often mixed, signalling lack of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of worn metaphors: 'Ring the changes on', 'take up the cudgel for', 'toe the line', 'ride roughshod over', 'stand shoulder to shoulder with', 'play into the hands of', 'no axe to grind', 'grist to the mill', 'fishing in troubled waters', 'on the order of the day', 'Achilles’ heel', 'swan song', 'hotbed'. Avoid using metaphors/similes you are used to seeing in print; prefer newly-invented or precise imagery. Be careful not to pervert original meanings (e.g. 'toe the line' → 'tow the line').

rubrics_metrics.name: Operators or verbal false limbs (nounifications and padded phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrases that pad sentences and eliminate simple verbs — noun constructions and general-purpose verbs replace direct verbs and obscure meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic phrases to avoid: 'render inoperative', 'militate against', 'make contact with', 'be subjected to', 'give rise to', 'have the effect of', 'play a leading part (role) in', 'make itself felt', 'take effect', 'exhibit a tendency to', 'serve the purpose of'. Use single-word verbs (break, stop, spoil, mend, kill) instead of periphrastic constructions; avoid turning verbs into nouns (by examination → by examining). Watch for '-ize' and 'de-' formations and gratuitous 'not un-' constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretentious diction (Latinate/foreign/jargon dress-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use Latinate, Greek, or foreign words simply to sound grand or scientific; these dress up simple statements and increase slovenliness and vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of pretentious words and phrases: 'phenomenon', 'element', 'individual', 'objective', 'categorical', 'effective', 'virtual', 'basic', 'primary', 'promote', 'constitute', 'exhibit', 'exploit', 'utilize', 'eliminate', 'liquidate', and adjectives like 'epoch-making', 'epic', 'historic', 'unforgettable', 'triumphant'. Foreign expressions flagged: 'cul de sac', 'ancien regime', 'deus ex machina', 'mutatis mutandis', 'status quo', 'gleichschaltung', 'weltanschauung'. Avoid inventing Latinate words ('deregionalize', 'impermissible', etc.) when plain English will do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningless or vague words (jargon and variable-meaning words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid words that are used without pointing to any discoverable object or that have multiple, incompatible meanings and are often used dishonestly or carelessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in art criticism — 'romantic', 'plastic', 'values', 'human', 'dead', 'sentimental', 'natural', 'vitality'; political words often abused: 'Fascism' (used to mean 'something not desirable'), 'democracy', 'socialism', 'freedom', 'patriotic', 'realistic', 'justice', 'class', 'totalitarian', 'science', 'progressive', 'reactionary', 'bourgeois', 'equality'. Tie words to precise meanings or discoverable objects; do not allow private definitions to be masked as common meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staleness of imagery and lack of precision; preference for concreteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern prose tends toward abstract, hackneyed phrasing and away from concreteness; this causes vagueness and loss of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete illustrations and vivid images (Orwell contrasts Ecclesiastes' concrete imagery with a Latinate abstract paraphrase). Compose by visualizing concrete objects before choosing words; aim for fresh, arresting phrases rather than ready‑made strips of words. Ask whether your sentence conjures clear images rather than generic abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ready-made phrases and clichés that make you think less
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't let prefabricated phrases construct your sentences and thoughts for you; ready-made tags anesthetize thought and conceal meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of ready-made tags: 'a consideration which we should do well to bear in mind', 'a conclusion to which all of us would readily assent', 'lay the foundations', 'achieve a radical transformation'. Be constantly on guard against them; if a phrase feels automatic, rework it to express a specific meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed metaphors (clashing images combined) indicate the writer is not forming a clear mental image of what they name and thus not thinking clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of mixed metaphor: 'The Fascist octopus has sung its swan song, the jackboot is thrown into the melting pot.' Ensure metaphorical images are coherent and illuminate rather than clash confusingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of euphemism and inflated style used to obscure or defend the indefensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Political writing frequently uses euphemism, question-begging and vague wording to name things without calling up their mental pictures; inflated language functions as a cover for insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'pacification' for bombardment and destruction, 'transfer of population' or 'rectification of frontiers' for forced removal, 'elimination of unreliable elements' for imprisonment or execution. Recognize and avoid language that blurs or conceals brutal facts; prefer direct phrasing that makes the reality visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-check questions for each sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A scrupulous writer should interrogate each sentence to ensure clarity, precision and freshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions Orwell recommends asking for every sentence: 'What am I trying to say? What words will express it? What image or idiom will make it clearer? Is this image fresh enough to have an effect?' He also suggests asking two more: 'Could I put it more shortly? Have I said anything that is avoidably ugly?' Use these as a routine checklist while composing and revising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the meaning choose the word (not vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words to fit the precise meaning you intend, rather than selecting words because they are fashionable or readily available in the existing dialect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When thinking of concrete objects, delay verbalization until the picture is clear; for abstract ideas, work to clarify meaning with images and sensations before accepting standard phrases. This reduces stale or mixed images, needless repetitions, humbug, and vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech you are used to seeing in print
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on familiar printed figures of speech; they are likely worn-out and unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Orwell's first explicit rule — avoid clichés and overused figurative language even if common in print. Prefer fresh, personally felt imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: Never use a long word where a short one will do
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer short, simple words to long Latinate or obscure words when they will convey the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Orwell's second rule — choose the fewest and shortest words that will cover your meaning; do not assume Latin/Greek roots are superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate unnecessary words to increase clarity and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Orwell's third rule — be economical: remove redundant or filler words and avoid periphrasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: Never use the passive where you can use the active
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor the active voice to make authorship and action clear and to avoid vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Orwell's fourth rule — avoid passive constructions which often obscure agents and blame; prefer direct active verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word, or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use everyday English equivalents instead of foreign, scientific, or jargon terms where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Orwell's fifth rule — avoid unnecessary foreign expressions and specialist jargon that distance or confuse readers; prefer plain English equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules are tools; if rigid adherence produces a barbarous or misleading statement, violate a rule to preserve truth and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Orwell's sixth and catch-all rule — do not let rules become ends in themselves; prefer honesty and lucidity even at the cost of occasional rule-bending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious action can improve language (kill stupid phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language change can be effected deliberately by a minority that jeers or refuses to use silly expressions; degeneracy is not entirely inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orwell cites examples — 'explore every avenue' and 'leave no stone unturned' were killed by journalists' jeers — and urges making pretentiousness unfashionable by conscious refusal to use flyblown metaphors, the 'not un-' formation, and gratuitous Latin/Greekisms.
